Float64frombits.configurations: Native Go directly calls math.Float64frombits and reads its storage bytes independently of math.Float64bits. The check also calls math.Float64bits to exercise the round-trip. Both normal compilation and compilation with intrinsics disabled are checked.

frexp.claim: Returns the exact fraction word and exponent, including unchanged words and exponent zero for signed zeros, infinities and NaNs. Normal fractions retain their original sign and payload with exponent field 1022. Subnormals normalize their payload and adjust the returned exponent.
frexp.limits: Reuses the model of the generic helper and its kernel proof of exact field arithmetic. The exact multiply by 2^52 during normalization is represented by its resulting fields. The check compares 336 boundaries and 60,000 sampled words with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537, forcing an exponent of zero in alternating samples.
frexp.configurations: Native Go directly invokes private math.frexp within its original package through a test-only overlay, bypassing public math.Frexp dispatch.

Frexp.claim: Returns the unchanged representation and exponent zero for signed zeros, infinities and NaNs. Otherwise returns a fraction word with the original sign and exponent field 1022, with the original normal payload or the subnormal payload below the highest set bit shifted into place. The returned exponent compensates for normalization.
Frexp.limits: The input is a raw binary64 word represented as a natural number. The model represents the exact multiply by 2^52 of a nonzero subnormal by its normal binary64 fields. The proof shows the resulting pair equals the independent field arithmetic specification. Native floating-point and bit reinterpretation are compared on 336 boundaries and 60,000 sampled words using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537. Alternating samples force the exponent field to zero.
Frexp.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.Frexp on byte-constructed float64 values and observing its output through a native-endian byte oracle. Runs under normal compilation and with intrinsics disabled in math and the driver.

Ilogb.claim: Returns the unbiased leading exponent of every finite nonzero binary64 input, MinInt32 for either zero, and MaxInt32 for either infinity or any NaN.
Ilogb.limits: Models the result of normalization on the exponent field. Native floating-point normalization is checked through the public entry point. The check covers 232 boundaries including all subnormal leading bit positions and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Ilogb.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.Ilogb on float64 values built from native-endian bytes.

Inf.claim: Returns a binary64 value with sign bit set exactly for a negative input, all eleven exponent bits set, and all fraction bits clear.
Inf.limits: The model interprets the Go int as a signed mathematical integer and represents Float64frombits by the resulting bits. The theorem holds across all mathematical integers, including all Go int widths. The comparison uses nine native int boundary cases and 60,000 uniform samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Inf.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.Inf on signed ints and reading the complete binary64 result with Float64bits, both under normal compilation and with compiler intrinsics disabled.

IsInf.claim: Returns true exactly for positive infinity when sign is nonnegative or negative infinity when sign is nonpositive.
IsInf.limits: The theorem covers all binary64 encodings and models sign as an integer. It uses sign-bit operations on encodings for Abs and negation and an ordered encoding comparison for the threshold against MaxFloat64. The check compares these operations with native floating-point behavior using 112 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537. Floating-point exception flags are outside the claim.
IsInf.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.IsInf with all three sign classes, both under normal compilation and with compiler intrinsics disabled.

IsNaN.claim: Returns true exactly for the two binary64 NaN encoding intervals above positive and negative infinity, including both quiet and signaling NaNs.
IsNaN.limits: The model represents float64 by its raw binary64 encoding and interprets the source self-comparison using a definition of binary64 numeric equality. The theorem covers every encoding. Hardware comparison equivalence is tested on 276 generated boundary cases and 60,000 uniform samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537. Floating-point exception flags are outside the claim.
IsNaN.configurations: Native Go calling math.IsNaN directly on float64 values constructed with Float64frombits.

ldexp.claim: Returns the exact binary64 word from scaling by the wrapped leading exponent, rounding denormal results to nearest even and preserving signed zero, infinity, and NaN words.
ldexp.limits: Reuses the generic helper model and kernel proof of wrapped exponent arithmetic and exact coefficient rounding. Represents normalization and multiplication by a power of two through integer shifts and nearest-even rounding. The independent math/big.Float oracle checks 608 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537. FINDINGS.md retains the unrestricted scaling-law counterexamples.
ldexp.configurations: Native Go directly invokes private math.ldexp within its original package through a test-only overlay, bypassing public math.Ldexp dispatch. The driver supplies the native int width.

Ldexp.claim: Returns the exact binary64 word from scaling by the wrapped leading exponent, with nearest-even rounding for denormal results and unchanged words for zeros, infinities and NaNs.
Ldexp.limits: The model uses raw binary64 words and the native Go int width. It abstracts normalization and the final exact power-of-two multiplication by integer shifts and nearest-even rounding. Lean reduces staged arithmetic to one wrapped addition and an exact coefficient formula and proves the four signed extrema witnesses for both 32- and 64-bit model widths. A math/big.Float oracle checks the wrapped behavior on 608 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537. The Go-only contract pilot checks the unrestricted scaling claim independently of the model.
Ldexp.configurations: Native Go calling math.Ldexp directly, with byte-wise storage observation, in normal and intrinsics-disabled compilation.

Logb.claim: Returns the exact finite binary exponent, including for subnormals. Both zeros become negative infinity, both infinities become positive infinity, and NaN words are preserved.
Logb.limits: Models binary64 input words. A finite result is represented by its integral exponent and the driver checks the exact float64 encoding of that integer, including positive zero for exponent zero. Exceptional results retain their raw output words. The driver checks 232 boundaries, including each possible highest subnormal bit at both signs, and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Logb.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.Logb with inputs constructed and outputs observed in native-endian binary64 storage.

max.claim: Returns positive infinity when either argument is positive infinity. Otherwise it returns Go's canonical NaN word when either input is a NaN, or the greater ordered word with positive zero preferred over negative zero.
max.limits: Reuses the generic source branch model and its kernel-checked order-key characterization. Checks exact output bits including the canonical NaN word on 576 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
max.configurations: Native Go directly invokes the private math.max helper within its original package through a test-only overlay, bypassing public math.Max dispatch.

Max.claim: Returns positive infinity when either argument is positive infinity. Otherwise it returns a NaN when either input is a NaN, or the greater ordered word with positive zero preferred over negative zero.
Max.limits: Proves the exact result of the generic source branches using the unsigned binary64 order key. The public Go comparison checks exact non-NaN output bits and NaN classification because architecture code may select a different payload. The check covers 576 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Max.configurations: Native Go calls math.Max directly under normal and intrinsics-disabled compilation. Architecture assembly can remain selected.

min.claim: Returns negative infinity when either argument is negative infinity. Otherwise it returns Go's canonical NaN word when either input is a NaN, or the smaller ordered word with negative zero preferred over positive zero.
min.limits: Reuses the generic source branch model and its kernel-checked order-key characterization. Checks exact output bits including the canonical NaN word on 576 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
min.configurations: Native Go directly invokes the private math.min helper within its original package through a test-only overlay, bypassing public math.Min dispatch.

Min.claim: Returns negative infinity when either argument is negative infinity. Otherwise it returns a NaN when either input is a NaN, or the smaller ordered word with negative zero preferred over positive zero.
Min.limits: Proves the exact result of the generic source branches using the unsigned binary64 order key. The public Go comparison checks exact non-NaN output bits and NaN classification because architecture code may select a different payload. The check covers 576 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Min.configurations: Native Go calls math.Min directly under normal and intrinsics-disabled compilation. Architecture assembly can remain selected.

NaN.claim: Returns the binary64 encoding with sign zero, exponent 2047, quiet bit set, and remaining payload equal to one.
NaN.limits: Exhausts the only input to this nullary function. The model represents Float64frombits by the resulting word. The comparison checks all 64 bits of the observed result on the execution platform, including the NaN payload.
NaN.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.NaN and reading the result with Float64bits under normal compilation and with compiler intrinsics disabled.

Nextafter.claim: Returns the adjacent binary64 rank toward the target, preserving the original sign when a step reaches zero. Equal numerical values return the first encoding. Either NaN input returns the pinned NaN encoding.
Nextafter.limits: Models comparisons and storage through raw binary64 order. The kernel proves the exact rank step and the output word bound. The comparison checks 576 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537, mixing identical, neighboring and independent encodings.
Nextafter.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.Nextafter on byte-constructed binary64 values, with normal and intrinsics-disabled compilation.

Nextafter32.claim: Returns the adjacent binary32 rank toward the target, preserving the original sign when a step reaches zero. Equal numerical values return the first encoding. Either NaN input returns the pinned narrowed quiet NaN.
Nextafter32.limits: The model represents widening by its NaN classification and sign effects and summarizes narrowing of the pinned quiet NaN as the observed binary32 encoding. The kernel proves the rank step and output word bound. The comparison checks 576 boundary pairs and 60,000 sampled pairs using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537, mixing identical, neighboring and independent encodings.
Nextafter32.configurations: Native Go directly calling math.Nextafter32 on float32 inputs constructed from native-endian bytes and observing the result bytes, with normal and intrinsics-disabled compilation.

lz.claim: Counts the leading zero bits of the unsigned 128-bit word formed by concatenating its high and low inputs, returning 128 when both words are zero.
lz.limits: The Lean theorem characterizes all input pairs by the minimum bit width of their combined value. The Go driver checks 257 boundary cases and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537 against an independent descending bit scan.
lz.configurations: Native Go invokes the private math.lz in its original package through test-only overlay fixtures. The fixed input widths are uint64 and the Go result is int32.

split.claim: Extracts the sign, preserves each nonzero exponent field and prepends its implicit significand bit, normalizes nonzero subnormal significands, and returns exponent -52 with zero significand for signed zeros.
split.limits: The theorem covers all raw 64-bit words, including infinity and NaN fields treated as raw encodings by the helper. The comparison checks 336 boundaries and 60,000 sampled words using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537. It uses repeated exact doubling as an independent normalization oracle.
split.configurations: Native Go invokes the private math.split helper in its original package through test-only overlay fixtures. Results are compared as raw uint32, int32 and uint64 fields.

nonzero.claim: Returns the uint64 word 1 whenever any input bit is set, and 0 when the input is all zero.
nonzero.limits: The theorem proves equivalence to the branchless complement of the zero indicator documented beside the Go helper, for all uint64 words. Go checks 258 boundary cases and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537, including zero, sparse and arbitrary words.
nonzero.configurations: Native Go invokes the private math.nonzero helper in its original package through test-only overlay fixtures.

zero.claim: Returns the uint64 word 1 when the input is all zero, and 0 whenever any input bit is set.
zero.limits: The Lean theorem proves equivalence to the branchless folding and unsigned subtraction formula documented in the Go source for all uint64 words. The Go comparison checks 258 boundary cases and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537, including arbitrary words, sparse words and zero.
zero.configurations: Native Go calls the private math.zero helper in its original package through test-only overlay fixtures.

isNegInt.claim: Returns true exactly for strictly negative finite integers. Both signed zeros, positive values, nonintegral inputs, infinities and NaNs return false.
isNegInt.limits: The model summarizes Modf’s finite zero-fraction test by comparing the input and truncated words. The kernel theorem characterizes all input encodings by sign, finite exponent and fractional residue. The math/big rational oracle checks 518 boundaries and 60,000 sampled words using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
isNegInt.configurations: Native Go invokes the private math.isNegInt in its original package through test-only overlay fixtures, passing raw binary64 encodings through Float64frombits.

isOddInt.claim: Returns true exactly when the binary64 input is a finite odd integer, for either sign. Magnitudes at least 2^53, nonintegral inputs, signed zeros, infinities and NaNs return false.
isOddInt.limits: The model uses the truncated word to test Modf's zero fraction and computes the low parity bit from the magnitude's integer conversion. The kernel theorem characterizes all encodings by exponent, fractional residue and quotient parity. The math/big rational oracle checks 470 boundaries and 60,000 sampled words using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
isOddInt.configurations: Native Go invokes the private math.isOddInt in its original package through test-only overlay fixtures, passing raw binary64 words through Float64frombits.

Modf.claim: Returns the truncated integer part and exact fractional remainder of finite inputs, retaining the input sign on both results. An infinite input returns the original infinity and a NaN fraction. A NaN input returns two NaNs.
Modf.limits: The Lean model represents the finite floating subtraction and sign copy by exact word arithmetic. The theorem gives the integer-word mask and a normalized residue formula. The rational oracle checks exact result bits for non-NaNs and NaN classification. It covers 672 boundaries and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537. NaN signs and payloads are outside the comparison.
Modf.configurations: Native Go directly calls math.Modf normally and with compiler intrinsics disabled in the driver and math package. This changes compilation of delegated operations; architecture code can still run.

Dim.claim: Returns positive zero when the binary64 subtraction x - y compares nonpositive, and otherwise returns that subtraction result. NaN inputs and same-sign infinity pairs produce NaN.
Dim.limits: The proof characterizes the clamp and pass-through at the modeled Lean Float operations. Cross-runtime subtraction and comparison semantics are tested by an exact rational oracle and special cases. NaN payloads and signs are outside the comparison. The driver checks 784 boundary pairs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Dim.configurations: Native Go directly calls math.Dim on raw binary64 pairs and compares exact result bits or NaN classification.

Pow10.claim: Returns positive zero below -323 and positive infinity above 308. Within the calculation interval it rounds the product of the positive block and offset powers, or the quotient of the negative block and positive offset powers, using the stored binary64 table values.
Pow10.limits: The kernel proves the constant tails and the quotient/remainder lookup partition for all integer inputs. Lean Float literal conversion and arithmetic are checked against a rational oracle that rounds the operands and final result separately. The comparison exhausts the 632 exponents in the calculation interval, checks eight tail cases and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Pow10.configurations: Native Go directly calls math.Pow10 on native int exponents and compares exact binary64 result words.

sqrt.claim: The generic moving-bit square root returns the correctly rounded result for positive finite binary64 inputs, preserves signed zeros and positive infinity, and returns a NaN for negative inputs or NaNs.
sqrt.limits: Shares the existing kernel proof of the moving-bit loop, exact integer remainder and rounding for math.Sqrt. This comparison calls the private Go helper directly and checks the integer square-root formula with math/big.Int. Exact result bits are compared except that NaN results are compared by class. The driver covers 12,612 boundaries and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
sqrt.configurations: Native Go directly invokes math.sqrt within its original package through test-only overlay fixtures, bypassing any substitution of the public math.Sqrt call.

Sqrt.claim: Returns the correctly rounded binary64 square root for positive finite inputs. Preserves signed zeros and positive infinity. Negative inputs and NaNs produce NaN.
Sqrt.limits: The model uses natural arithmetic for the generic moving-bit loop and a leading-bit calculation for subnormal normalization. The kernel proves the digit loop computes the integer square root and exact remainder of the normalized scaled radicand, and gives the final rounding formula. The separate math/big.Float oracle checks exact non-NaN words and NaN classification, including 12,612 boundaries and 60,000 sampled inputs with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Sqrt.configurations: Native Go directly calls math.Sqrt in the normal compilation profile and with compiler intrinsics disabled in the driver and math package.

RoundToEven.claim: Rounds to the nearest integer with ties to an even integer. Preserves the input sign when the result is zero. Integral inputs and infinities pass through, and NaN inputs return NaNs.
RoundToEven.limits: The Lean theorem proves a quotient, fractional residue and parity formula for all binary64 words. The model collapses the shifts whose values vanish at integral or special exponents. Native NaN payload and sign are outside the comparison. The driver checks 1,086 boundaries and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537, including halfway points adjacent to even and odd integers.
RoundToEven.configurations: Native Go calls math.RoundToEven directly under normal compilation and again with compiler intrinsics disabled in the driver and the math package.

Signbit.claim: Returns true exactly when bit 63 of the IEEE 754 binary64 representation is set, including negative zero and NaN encodings with the sign bit set.
Signbit.limits: The proof covers all 64-bit representations and takes the result of Float64bits as input. The check constructs native float64 values with Float64frombits and exercises reinterpreting them through Signbit with 258 boundary cases and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Signbit.configurations: Native Go calling math.Signbit directly with normal compilation and compiler intrinsics disabled.

ilogb.claim: Returns the leading exponent of every finite nonzero binary64 input, including subnormals.
ilogb.limits: Matches the helper's finite nonzero precondition. Go and Lean are compared on 216 boundaries and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
ilogb.configurations: Native pinned Go calls the private helper through a test-only bridge and compares with the independent leading-bit oracle.

normalize.claim: Returns the unchanged word and adjustment zero for normals. For nonzero subnormals, returns the exact word after scaling by 2^52 and adjustment -52.
normalize.limits: Matches the helper's finite nonzero precondition. Tests 216 boundaries including every subnormal leading-bit position on both signs and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
normalize.configurations: Native pinned Go calls the private helper through a test-only bridge and compares the exact stored result and adjustment.

trunc.claim: Truncates finite inputs toward zero, preserving the sign of a zero result. Integral words, infinities, and NaN sign and payload bits are unchanged by the generic helper.
trunc.limits: Reuses the all-word kernel theorem for the generic exponent and mask implementation. The direct Go comparison checks exact words against the quotient formula and an independent numeric conversion oracle. It checks 672 boundary inputs and 60,000 samples using seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
trunc.configurations: Native Go calls private math.trunc in its original package through test-only overlay fixtures, bypassing the public Trunc architecture dispatch and intrinsic.

Trunc.claim: Truncates toward zero, retaining the input sign when the result is zero. Integral encodings and infinities remain unchanged, and NaN inputs return NaNs.
Trunc.limits: The Lean theorem proves the raw-word formula for the generic exponent and mask implementation. Native Trunc may use a compiler intrinsic or architecture assembly, which are tested for exact non-NaN result words and NaN classification. NaN payload and sign on hardware paths are outside the comparison. The driver checks 94 boundaries and 60,000 samples with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537, including 30,000 words sampled across the fractional exponent range and its transitions.
Trunc.configurations: Native Go calls math.Trunc directly with normal compilation and with compiler intrinsics disabled. Disabling intrinsics may still select the architecture assembly in the Go wrapper.

Floor.claim: Returns the greatest integer no greater than the input for finite inputs, preserving signed zero. Infinities are unchanged and NaNs remain NaN.
Floor.limits: The kernel proves the generic encoded fraction-rounding formula. The rational oracle checks exact non-NaN words, with NaNs checked by class. The comparison uses 94 boundaries and 60,000 inputs with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Floor.configurations: Native Go directly calls math.Floor with normal compilation and with intrinsics disabled in the driver and math package. Both runs also call private floor and ceil through a test-only overlay with normal compiler settings. Public wrappers can still select architecture code.

Ceil.claim: Returns the least integer no less than the input for finite inputs, preserving signed zero. Infinities are unchanged and NaNs remain NaN.
Ceil.limits: The kernel proves the generic encoded fraction-rounding formula. The rational oracle checks exact non-NaN words, with NaNs checked by class. The comparison uses 94 boundaries and 60,000 inputs with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
Ceil.configurations: Native Go directly calls math.Ceil with normal compilation and with intrinsics disabled in the driver and math package. Both runs also call private floor and ceil through a test-only overlay with normal compiler settings. Public wrappers can still select architecture code.

floor.claim: Returns the greatest integer no greater than the input for finite inputs, preserving signed zero. Infinities are unchanged and NaNs remain NaN.
floor.limits: The kernel proves the generic encoded fraction-rounding formula. The rational oracle checks exact non-NaN words, with NaNs checked by class. The comparison uses 94 boundaries and 60,000 inputs with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
floor.configurations: Native pinned Go directly calls math.floor through the test-only bridge.

ceil.limits: The kernel proves the generic encoded fraction-rounding formula. The rational oracle checks exact non-NaN words, with NaNs checked by class. The comparison uses 94 boundaries and 60,000 inputs with seeds 17, 2718 and 65537.
